**My reasoning:**

My family has farmed this land in Quzhou for three generations. I have about 8 mu of flatland here on the North China Plain. There is really only one system that makes sense for land like mine: winter wheat followed by summer maize. Every family on my street does this rotation. The soil knows it, and so do I after thirty years of doing it myself.

For wheat, I will plant Jimai variety — the seed shop in town sells it and my neighbor got good results last year. I always rotary-till the field after I harvest the maize in October before sowing wheat. Wheat needs water, especially in spring when it is jointing. I irrigate before winter sets in, then again at jointing, then once more around heading. Three times usually. I hire someone to spray herbicide in spring and treat for aphids before harvest.

For maize, I direct-seed it into the wheat stubble right after the June harvest — no time to till, and the maize doesn't need it. I buy Xianyu 335 hybrid seed. It costs more but the yield makes it worth it. Maize usually gets enough rain here in July and August, but if there is a dry spell in July I will pump from the well once. I spray once for corn borer if I see the damage.

My fertilizer I apply mostly as compound fertilizer at planting, then add urea as topdressing. I know the extension station says I use too much nitrogen but this is what my father did and what my neighbors do, and I am not going to risk a bad harvest to experiment.

decision.reasoning_summary: As a 52-year-old woman farming 8 mu of flatland in Quzhou County, I will follow the winter wheat and summer maize rotation that defines this part of Hebei. I plant improved wheat varieties and hybrid maize seed because the yields justify the cost. Wheat gets rotary tillage in autumn and three irrigations across the season; maize is direct-seeded into stubble after wheat harvest and receives one irrigation if July turns dry. Fertilizer rates follow what my neighbors and my own experience suggest is safe — compound fertilizer at planting and urea topdressing — accepting that I may apply more nitrogen than strictly necessary in order to protect the harvest I depend on.
